Post Title: PRD vs PMRD and why PMMs need to build one.
Body:
As a PM, I never started without a PRD.
As a PMM, I always started without a PMRD.
I have done both jobs. Here's what PMM function is really missing.👇

PMRD - "Product Marketing Requirement Document"

Maybe nothing like PMRD exists, but honestly....why not???

If you are in tech/SaaS world (Product manager or not), you probably know this.

Even before a single line of code gets written, PMs write a PRD - a Product Requirements Document.

What are they building.
What's in scope
What's not.
For whom.
Why.

But in Product marketing, nothing equivalent exists.

As PMMs, we do all the upstream thinking - positioning, messaging, differentiation, who we're for, who we're not for, GTM strategy, what channels to target, market research, etc.

And despite all this work being super critical to run the entire GTM motion, it lives in scattered documents with one slide deck here, another strategy doc there.

So, here's what I think we are missing.

"Product Marketing Requirement Document" - a PMRD

And, to make things simpler, I drew a parallel with good old PRD.

Post Title: "SaaS is dead, with AI you can build any tool." Is this what you really think???
Body:
"SaaS is dead, with AI you can build any tool."
Is this what you really think???
If yes, you need to read this. 

So, I can make Ghee (clarified butter) out of milk at home, but that doesn't means I'll do it.

I can, also, grow veggies in my home garden, but that doesn't means I'll do it.

Not because I can't.

Because that's not my core job, 
that's not where I make money.

And the money I'd save by doing it is certainly not a great time tradeoff I would be making.

I hope you got the point.

So, just because you can build an internal tool with AI to solve some business workflow, doesn't mean you should deviate from your core product/business to do it.

Your primary source of revenue will always be your core product and not the SaaS tool you built to save money on the subscription.

Remember, 
No business becomes cash rich by saving money, 
it becomes cash rich by investing right, innovating right, and executing right.

Build the thing only you can build.
You can buy the rest.

Post Title: One question that almost always get asked in a PMM interview...
Body:
One question that almost always get asked in a PMM interview and answered with all the vagueness possible...

Question: What is Product Marketing?
(or some or the other variation of it)

Answer you get?

Product marketing bridges the gap between product, sales, etc. etc.
Product marketing builds strategic foundations.
Product marketing shapes how market understands the product.

Okay. All this is fine and good-to-hear kinda things. 

And while they aren't incorrect but,
they doesn't explain anything concrete about the role.

So then, what is product marketing?

If you ask me, this is how I put it - 

Product marketing is mix of 4 core pillars - 

1. Marketing Foundations
The whole positioning, messaging, defining the ICP, competitive intelligence, market research, all comes under it.

2. Product Portfolio Success
Driving adoption, expansion, retention, working with Customer Success teams, basically the whole customer lifecycle marketing. Also, regular feedback to product teams and influencing the product roadmap.

3. Sales Enablement
Building sales playbooks, sales narratives, case studies, product collaterals, SDR training, battlecards, etc. Everything that helps deal close faster.

4. GTM 
Product launches, running campaigns, channel mix identification based on the stage, events support, analyst relations. 

Think of any product marketing deliverable and 
it can be put under one of these 4 buckets,

and, simply put, that's what product marketing is all about.
(at an operator level)

If all 4 of them are done right,
here are the 3 core outcomes one can expect - 

1. Reduction in overall sales cycle
2. Increase in deal win rate
3. Improvement in deal quality

So, if you are fellow PMM (or an aspiring one), structure your answer around the 4 buckets.

And, if you are a founder hiring your first PMM, 
use the 4 buckets to scope the role 
and the 3 outcomes to measure them.

Hope this helps and removes the vagueness from one of the most asked PMM interview question.

Post Title: "Strategy" is the most misunderstood term amongst SaaS founders.
Body:
After 5+ years in B2B SaaS, I am 100% convinced that word "Strategy" is the most misunderstood term amongst SaaS founders.
Why I say so?

Because when marketing strategy is discussed,
this is what I hear most:

- run campaigns
- activate new channels
- product demos
- launches
- webinars
- demand gen

.....the list can go on.

But all these, in principal, are "tactics".

The foundations on which these run is "Strategy".

Let's take a short dive into business literature.

To double check how "Strategy" is defined,
(and flex my B-school degree, kidding!)

I literally pulled out my textbook on the course "Strategy".
And here's what it said:

[Strategy is a deliberate set of choices that positions an organization to achieve a sustainable competitive advantage and superior long-term performance relative to its competitors]

----------------------------

Then I went a step further to find how marketing gurus explain the term "Strategy".

> Roger L. Martin (In his book "Playing to Win")
"Strategy is an integrated cascade of choices that tells you what game you're playing, where you will play it, and how you will win."

> Seth Godin
"It's a philosophy of becoming. I don't think it's a set of tactics. I don't think it's about winning in the short run. I think it's about being very clear about the change we seek to make and who we seek to change."

> Michael Porter
"Operational effectiveness is not strategy."

Did you notice the common thread?

Choices.
Positioning.
Where to play.
Who to change.

----------------------------

So, in the most fundamental sense,

Strategy is:

- positioning you want to take in the market
- to decide which category you want to compete in
- to decide for whom you are
- to decide for whom you are not
- to decide which channels to go after

How to execute it is when campaigns, activating channels, launches, etc. come into picture.

====================

If you are a SaaS founder reading this,
and is trapped in "tactics" disguised as "strategy".

It's time you take action.

Post Title: The one thing I changed that actually made my client's sales pitch decks Unignorable
Body:
The one thing I changed that actually made my client's sales pitch decks Unignorable...
(working for 20+ pitch decks already)

"Making the prospect the hero of the pitch,
and not otherwise"

Most sales pitch decks i see start with
putting the company at the centre of discussion.

They start with:
- about us
- investor & customer logos
- awards, G2 & analyst mentions
- scale & impact numbers

By now, the prospect is 10 minutes into the call,
and yet not been a point of discussion.

Remember,
Every slide on the deck should be about prospect's transformation and not yours.

You're the guide and they're the ones going on the journey with you.

------------------------------------

Here are 7 rules I run every client sales pitch deck through.

And all of them enforce one principle,
"Prospect is the Hero"

1. Never start with you.
No logo wall. No "About us." No investor names. No brags.
Start with what's changing in the buyer's world.
Market shift, operational reality, environment.

2. Paint the future state.
What does the prospect's life look like once their problem is solved?
That picture should be compelling enough for them to look for a solution.

3. Every product feature must solve a named problem.
Don't list capabilities.
Instead, tie each one to a specific pain already established in the pitch.

4. Proof comes after persuasion.
Customer logos, testimonials on slide 3 & 4 would do nothing.
Show them once the buyer already agrees the problem is real and worth solving.

5. The deck must match the rest of your story.
The website homepage, the LinkedIn posts, all should tell the same story.
If your deck says one thing and your website says another, that's red flag.

6. Every insight should lead back to why YOU.
If your reframe points to a problem your competitor solves equally well,
you have technically educated the prospect for free.
Your insight should make your differentiated capabilities the only logical answer.

7. Quantify what happens if they do nothing.
Do not put generic statements like "you will fall behind."
Instead give them a calculation on what they are leaving on the table.
Hard numbers always create urgency.

------------------------------------

Keep these 7 points in mind while building your next sales pitch deck.

And if you want the slide by slide structure, I can share that too.

DM me.

Post Title: Your biggest competition is not your closest competitor. But...
Body:
In a recent client conversation, I realised their biggest competition was NOT their closest competitor. But...

"Inaction"

Their prospect's decision to just...not do anything.

And it reminded me of a lecture from B-school
on consumer psychology. Prof said:

Netflix's biggest competition isn't Prime video,
but sleep.

Coke's biggest competition isn't Pepsi,
but water.

In both the cases, people pick the default option.
Technically, the option that doesn't require them to make a decision.

Why?
Because inaction is an easy choice.

And in case of B2B Software purchases
where stakes are high,
the contract is annual,
and the buyer has to convince 3 other stakeholders.

Inaction is THE easiest and safest choice.

And, here's how to win over this fierce competitor:

"Help"

Yes, help your buyer take a decision.

- Show what outcomes you can help them achieve
- Show the cost of inaction or going with status-quo
- Help them understand the market better
- Help them know the real alternatives

The least you need to do is to:
- talk about your company/product in isolation
- bombard them with your "cutting-edge" features

These come later.
You first need to consult them right.
Give them confidence to break the "Do Nothing" barrier.

Approach your homepage, sales pitch to break that barrier.

Post Title: 4 weeks ago, I had an interesting observation at my gym.
Body:
4 weeks ago, I had an interesting observation at my gym.
Wanted to validate it before making any conclusions.
So I observed it for the next 4 weeks.

It was a Monday.
Hit the gym around 8 AM (probably the most crowded slot)
And I had an hour to finish my workout because of some in-person meetings lined-up for the day.

Just like most people, I used to do push day on Mondays - chest, triceps.

But that day, since the bench press and chest fly were over-occupied,
I decided to do legs instead.
(also because I had skipped legs the previous week)

And to my shock,
Bareely anyone was doing a legs workout.

I finished my session in under an hour.
Like you would on a random Tuesday 3 PM when the gym is almost empty.
(If your schedule/work allows ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ¬)

But I kept thinking - why does almost everyone rush to do chest workout on a Monday morning?

So I googled it. Asked ChatGPT. Here's what I found ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Upper-body workouts produce faster visible changes (arms, chest) - more immediate feeling of accomplishment.
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Monday = high motivation. Chest feels like a "worthy" opener to the week.
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Social proof - everyone does chest on Monday, so it must be the right way.

The 3rd reason was so vivid,

Nobody consciously decided "Monday = Chest day."
It justÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ¦ evolved that way.
And now everyone follows it without questioning it.

And it got me thinking -
How often do we do things in a certain way just because we have been doing them like that?

And, I see this exact pattern with my SaaS clients.

They want to do what their closest competitor is doing.
Same homepage structure.
Similar messaging angles.
Same marketing campaigns.

And all of it leads to just one thing.
A sea of sameness.

You remove the logo and you can't differentiate between the 2 competitors.

P.S. - After 4 weeks of observing this "Monday = Chest Day" pattern,
I have permanently moved my legs workout to Monday.

Saves time.
I enjoy it more.

Post Title: I built a 10-parameter audit for B2B SaaS homepages.
Body:
I built a 10-parameter audit for B2B SaaS homepages.
And, It's the ONLY thing standing between your homepage and a higher conversion rate. ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ

----

I've been running this structure for every client engagement.

Last week i decided to pen it down.

10 clear parameters.
Not a "vibes check".
But a scorecard. Out of 50.
No subjectivity.
Pure Clarity.

Here are the 10 parameters ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ

1. Category Clarity
Can a visitor place your product in a known category within 5 seconds?

2. ICP Specificity
Does your hero tell the right person "this is for you" and signal to the wrong ones that it isn't?

3. Problem Framing
Is the problem stated from the buyer's point of view, not yours?

4. Value Proposition Clarity
Is there a clean capability ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ outcome link, or just feature dumps and vague outcome claims?

5. Differentiation
"Why you" over the 3 other competitors your prospects are considering?

6. Hero Section coherence
Do your headline, sub-headline, visual, and CTA work as a system or were they 4 unconnected pieces just floating around?

7. Messaging Hierarchy
Does the page flow as a persuasion sequence ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ Problem ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Capability ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Proof ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Action?

8. Social Proof Quality
Are your testimonials killing real objections, or just decorating the page?

9. Competitive Positioning
Does your copy speak to a buyer already evaluating alternatives, or pretend competitors don't exist?

10. Conversion Architecture
Is there a clear path for both the "ready to buy" and the "just researching" visitor?

----

Each parameter has a 1ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ5 scoring guide and the most common failure pattern I've seen repeatedly with early stage B2B SaaS companies.

Add them up, and you get a number out of 50 that tells you exactly where your homepage is leaking.

Post Title: Arriving at a positioning strategy and committing to it are two very different things.
Body:
Arriving at a positioning strategy and committing to it are two very different things.

Think about it like joining a gym.

You find the best gym.
You talk to few trainers there.
You watch multiple youtube videos.
You research the best workout program.

And you probably spend weeks figuring out the "right" plan.

And then - you start.

Week 3, you see no visible change. You switch programs.
Week 6, still no dramatic change. You try something new.
And six months later, you're still at square one.

Not because the programs were wrong.
But because you never gave any of them a real chance.

Positioning works exactly the same way.

SaaS founders spend months internally (or sometimes with agencies like ours) to arrive at a well-thought-through positioning strategy.

And the moment the pipeline doesn't explode in 60 days, they start tweaking.

Let's change the heropage headline.
Let's rewrite the value prop.
Let's shift the ICP.

All the above 3 btw are not even positioning iteration. ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ
That's "let's-try-something-else" kinda panic.

And I am not saying you should never iterate your positioning.
Here's when you should:

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ You're entering a new growth phase
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ You've decided to pivot
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Your overall strategy has fundamentally shifted

Until then?

Defend it.
Implement it consistently across every channel (website, sales deck, outbound, ads).

Positioning is a long-term game.

And like the gym - the results come to those who show up consistently, not to those who keep changing the plan.

And yes, I followed one simple plan and routine.

1800 Calories per day
120 Gms of protein per day

1 hour a day.

Post Title: Most SaaS discovery calls are a complete waste of time.

A discovery call has just one job,

Understand the prospect's world deeply enough
to know whether you can genuinely help them or not.

And if you can help, exactly how.

That's it.

Not to pitch.
Not to impress.
Just to understand.

----

Here are the questions you need to ask
categorised in 4 buckets -

1ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Their current situation

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ "Walk me through how you're currently handling [problem area]."
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ "What does that process look like end to end?"
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ "Which parts of it are working? Which aren't?"

2ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Their pain

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ "What's the biggest friction point in that process today?"
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ "What have you already tried to fix it?"
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ "What happened?"

3ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Current priorities

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ "Why is solving this a priority right now?"
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ "Who else is this affecting in the organisation?"

Post Title: Your sales pitch deck should never lead "with your product".
Body:
Your sales pitch deck should never lead "with your product".
It should lead "to your product".
There's a big difference and it's costing you deals. ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ

----

Here's what most B2B SaaS pitch decks look like:

Slide 1: Company Overview
Slide 2: Logo List of Marquee customers
Slide 3: Impact Numbers
Slide 4: Founding Team, List of Advisors
Slide 5: Our Investors, Global presence
Slide 6: Solution Intro
Slide 7-15: Features - Features - Features
Slide 16-19: Case Studies
Slide 20: "Any questions?"

The prospect is bored by Slide 3.
Disengaged by Slide 5.
And mentally checking out by Slide 9 or 10.

Not because your product is bad.
Because you skipped the most important part.

You never made them feel
that you understand their problem, their world well.

----

1ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Section 1: Set the Context
What's happening in the prospect's world right now?
Market shift, operational reality, environment.
This isn't about your company.
It's about showing you've done your homework on theirs.

----

2ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Section 2: The Problem
Name the specific pain - precisely.
The more specific you are,
the more the prospect leans in.
Specificity signals understanding.
Vagueness signals a generic pitch.

----

3ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Section 3: The Ideal Solution
Before you pitch your product,
explain what the ideal solution to this problem looks like.
This section educates the prospect
on what is the best way to solve their problem.

----

4ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Section 4: Cost of Inaction
The most underused slide in B2B SaaS decks.
What does doing nothing cost - today, in 6 months, in a year?
Urgency doesn't come from your product's features.
It comes from the cost of NOT solving the problem.

----

5ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Section 5: Your Product
Now, introduce your product.
Not as a feature list.
As the answer to everything you just built up.
"Here's how we solve exactly what we just walked through."
Connect every capability back to the problem.
Connect every feature back to the ideal solution you described.

----

6ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Section 6: Proof
Customer logos. Case studies. Quantified outcomes.
"Reduced manual reconciliation from 2 days to 2 hours."
"Saved the ops team 14 hours a week."
Specific results from real customers.

----

7ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Section 7: CTA
One clear next step.
"Let's run a pilot."
"Let's do a technical deep-dive."
"Start a 2-week trial."
Don't end with "any questions?"

----

The difference between a deck that closes
and a deck that gets a polite "We'll think about it and let you know" is:

One builds a narrative the prospect walks into.
The other presents a product the prospect has to evaluate.

Build the narrative first.
The product sells itself after that.

Post Title: How to define your ICP in 3 layers
Body:
500 target accounts ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ 12 replies ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ 1 demo.
That's what a firmographic-only ICP gets you.
Here's the 3-layer fix ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ

----

This is what most B2B SaaS teams do when defining their ICP ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ

They list "firmographics".

Industry: SaaS
Company size: 50ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ500 employees
Geography: North America
Revenue: $5MÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ$50M ARR

And they STOP there. ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ

Then they wonder why their SDRs are burning through the list
with almost no new conversations.

The problem isn't the list.
It's that firmographics alone can't tell you
whether a company actually needs your product right now.

A company can fit every firmographic criteria perfectly
and still have NO reason to buy from you.

----

So what's missing?

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Two layers that most ICP definitions skip entirely.

----

1ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Layer 1: Use Case

Define the specific workflow a company needs to be doing
in order to have a reason to use your product.

Not "they're in logistics."
But "they're manually doing route planning across multi-leg logistics operations"

Not "they're in HR tech."
But "they're running performance review cycles for teams of 50+ with no structured process."

The use case is the trigger.
It's what makes a company an active buyer.

If a company fits your firmographics but doesn't have a use case?
They're not your ICP. They just look like it.

----

2ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Layer 2: Product Category

Define the specific category your product belongs to -
and that your ICP would actively shop for.

This matters because buyers don't shop for random companies.
They shop for categories.

And when buyers can't categorise you,
they can't put you in a mental bucket.
When they can't put you in a mental bucket, they can't evaluate you.
When they can't evaluate you, they won't buy.

"We need a contract management tool."
"We're evaluating workforce planning software."
"We're looking for a freight visibility platform."

If a company isn't in the market for your product category,
no amount of outreach will create that need.

----

Now, is when you add your firmographics on top.

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Use Case + Category gives you the qualifying signal.
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Firmographics give you the targeting precision.

Together, they tell you:

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ This type of company
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Doing this specific workflow
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ In the market for this category of solution

That's a sharp ICP.
That's a list where every name has a real reason to buy.

----

The difference in output?

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ A firmographic-only ICP gives you volume (which fills your calendar)
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ A Use Case + Category + Firmographic ICP gives you a pipeline (which fills your CRM)

Post Title: Your homepage has 10 seconds to answer 4 questions.
Body:
Your homepage has 10 seconds to answer 4 questions.
Most B2B SaaS websites answer none of them.
Here's the exact homepage structure I use to fix that. ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ

The most common mistake B2B SaaS homepages do -

Trying to sound clever
before being clear.

Punchy taglines that say nothing.
Hero sections that talk about the company - not the customer.
Walls of feature lists with zero context on why it matters.

The result?

A prospect lands on your homepage.
Reads for 10 seconds.
Leaves - with no idea what you actually do.

That's not a design problem.
That's a messaging problem.

And it starts with not having a structured homepage framework.

So here's the one I use (and recommend) section-by-section.

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ

1ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ The Hero

This is the most valuable real estate on your entire website.

One job only - answer this instantly:
"What does this product do, and who is it for?"

No clever wordplay.
No vague vision statements.
Just radical clarity.

Your headline should complete this sentence in the prospect's head:
"Oh - so this is a [product category] for [ICP] that helps them [core outcome] through [core capability]"

If it can't do that - rewrite it.

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ

2ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Establish the Problem

Your prospect needs to feel understood before they'll trust you.

This section does one thing:
Show them you know their world better than they expected.

Name the specific problem.
Name the frustration that comes with it.
Name the cost of leaving it unsolved.

When a prospect reads this and thinks "that's exactly what I'm dealing with" -
you've earned the next scroll.

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ

3ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Establish the Solution

Now (and only now) introduce your product.

Not with features.
With the bridge.

"Here's how we solve exactly what you just read about."

Keep it tight. Keep it direct.
One crisp paragraph that connects the problem to what you do.

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ

4ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Differentiation / Use Cases / How It Works

This section changes based on what your product needs most.

If your product is easily confused with competitors ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ
lead with your 3 core differentiators.

If your product solves multiple distinct problems ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ
lead with 3 primary use cases.

If your product has a unique or non-obvious mechanism ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ
lead with a step-by-step "how it works."

Pick one. Go deep on it.
Don't try to do all three on one page.

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ

5ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Social Proof

By this point, your prospect understands what you do
and why it's different.

Now they need to know it actually works.

Testimonials. Quantified results.
"40% reduction in contract turnaround time."
"Saved 6 hours per week per rep."

Specific > generic. Always.

"Loved by 500+ companies" means nothing.
"Helped Acme close deals 2x faster" means everything.

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ

6ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ CTA

One ask. One action. No confusion.

Make it a logical next step one needs to take post reading the homepage.

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ

6 essential sections. One clear job each.
Every second a prospect spends on your homepage
should give them more clarity - not less.

Post Title: Here's how I run Positioning & Messaging process with every client.
Body:
Here's how I run Positioning & Messaging process with every client. ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ

2 weeks. 5 steps. 1 document that your entire GTM runs on.

ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ¾ Save this for later.

----

I've worked with multiple early-stage B2B SaaS startups.

And here's the pattern,

Companies jump straight to GTM channels -
SEO, paid ads, outbound, events.

Without ever answering the most fundamental question,
"Why should a customer pick us over everyone else?"

That's a core positioning question.
And most teams never sit down to answer it properly.

So here's the 5-step process that does exactly that.

----

1ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Step 1: Competitive Research

Before anything else - understand the battlefield.

I research up to 5 closest competitors.

For each, I map out:
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Which ICP they're targeting
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ What positioning angle they're taking
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Which product category they're competing in
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ What core problem they claim to solve
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ What differentiation they lead with
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ What their customers say on G2, Capterra, Gartner

----

2ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Step 2: Founder & Product Deep Dive

Research tells you what the market looks like.
This step tells you where you fit.

I run a detailed discussion with the founder & key stakeholders.

I aim to understand:
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Current positioning gaps they've already noticed
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Marketing challenges - unclear website, poor lead quality, long sales cycles
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Review everything that exists - pitch decks, demo videos, 1-pagers, sales collaterals

This step is where the real gold is.

Founders know things about their product that no competitor research will ever reveal.
The job is to pull it out.

----

3ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Step 3: Define the Positioning Elements

Now the synthesis begins.

Using Steps 1 and 2, I define:

Primary positioning elements -
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ product category to compete in
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Use cases the product solves
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Competitive alternatives

Secondary positioning elements -
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Target company type
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Buyer persona
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Desired outcome

From these, I first define
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ ICP
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ core problem the product solves
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ core differentiation
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ unique value it delivers

----

4ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Step 4: Build the Positioning Strategy

This is where everything comes together.

Using Steps 1, 2 and 3,
I develop a clear positioning strategy.

A deliberate point of view on:
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Which market to compete in
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Which customer to go after
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ How to be meaningfully different

----

5ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Step 5: Build the Positioning & Messaging 1-Pager

It clearly lays out:
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ The core problem being solved
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Sub-problems and use cases
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Product capabilities, features, and benefits
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ How the product differentiates in the market

With this,
Internally - Your sales, product, and marketing will finally speak the same language.

Externally - this becomes the website homepage, the sales pitch deck, and every other customer-facing asset.

That's the 2-week process.
From zero clarity to a positioning foundation your entire GTM runs on.

----

If your team is about to go to market,
or already in market but not getting the results you expected,

start here.

Post Title: How to differentiate an early stage B2B SaaS in a crowded market?
Body:
How to differentiate an early stage B2B SaaS in a crowded market?

Here are 9 proven ways in which you can do that ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ

And no, you need not slam "AI-powered" (for the sake of it)

or

Claim an outcome which your competitor aren't claiming yet
(because they can claim the same any fine day ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ¬)

---

But here's what you can actually do ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ  Hyper-Specific ICP (The "Who")
Narrow your focus, you instantly become the obvious choice for that specific group.
(ServiceTitan)

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ¡ Niche Use Case (The "What For")
Solve one high-stakes problem exceptionally well.
(Vanta)

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ¢ Target Geography (The "Where")
The US market might be saturated. But what about the DACH region? Or Southern Europe?
(Factorial HR)

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ Pricing Model (The "How Much")
If everyone in your category hides behind "Contact Sales" and annual lock-ins, offer transparent, usage-based pricing. Removing friction in how people pay is your biggest wedge.
(PostHog)

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ¤ Time-to-Value (The "Speed")
If your enterprise competitor takes 3 months to implement, and you can get them live in 3 days? That is a massive differentiator.
(Attio CRM)

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ¥ A Contrarian PoV (The "Why")
A strong, documented POV attracts your ideal buyers and actively repels the bad fits.
(Linear)

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ¦ Deep Ecosystem Integration (The "Connection")
Don't integrate with 50 tools poorly. Integrate with 1 tool flawlessly. Being the "No. 1 native app for Salesforce" or "The ultimate Shopify add-on" is a highly lucrative positioning strategy.
(Gorgias)

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ§ GTM Motion (The "How")
Are your competitors entirely Sales-led? Launch a frictionless PLG (Product-Led Growth) motion.
Are they pure PLG? Introduce a white-glove sales motion for buyers who want their hands held.
(Apollo[dot]io)

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ¨ ??? Couldn't think of 9th one ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂ§ÃÂ
If you had to add one more way to differentiate in a crowded market, what would it be? Let me know in the comments. ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ

---

P.S. - The companies mentioned above are used purely as examples to illustrate these differentiation strategies, based on my personal observations. In SaaS, positioning evolves with time, so their specific differentiators may have shifted over time.

Post Title: While positioning, clarity first, creativity second.
Body:
"Can we be creative in how we position ourselves?" asked a SaaS founder.

My honest answer? - a Big No.

To make your B2B SaaS stand out, trying to be "cool & creative" is the worst approach.

Here's Why ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ

Positioning is NOT the place for creativity.

Positioning is all about one thing: CLARITY

It's about bringing the absolute clarity needed to win in the market you compete in.

It should answer some of the hard questions:

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ What is your product?
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ For who is it? (And just as importantly, for who is it NOT?)
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ How do you differentiate?
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ What specific use case or problem does your product solve?
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ What is your unique PoV?

Once these hard questions are answered...

Your next step is figuring out how to explain all of this on your website homepage and sales pitch deck.

And THIS is where the creative part can come in: Copywriting.

But even here, you don't need to go crazy on creativity.

Your prospects aren't looking to read a piece of art.

They just want answers to their basic questions.

The only "cleverness" you should apply?

Making what you write memorable by using phrases, words, and ideas that stick even when they are off the page.

Clarity first.
Creativity second.

Post Title: Here's what AI should (and should NOT) do in Product Marketing
Body:
Now, this could be a debatable one but chuck it!
IMO, here's what AI should (and should NOT) do in Product Marketing ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ

As a Product Marketer, our job is to find the "Winning Narrative."

AI can for sure help you write it (atleast the base draft), but it cannot find it for you.

----------

Here is how I recommend (and use) AI in Product Marketing.

ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ What AI should do ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ (The "Execution")

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Competitive Intelligence
Feed it 10 competitor websites and ask it do an extensive research on it. It saves hours of manual scraping and gives you base to start with.

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Content Repurposing
I use NotebookLM for this.
Turn a 45-minute webinar transcript into 5 LinkedIn posts, a blog summary, and an email sequence in minutes.
Feed it sales call recordings, customer interviews - Play around, create valuable content out of it.

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ First-Draft Drafting
Give it your unique PoV, enough context, and your requirements. Get the first draft ready, refine it, edit it. It saves you hours wasted in getting started with the first draft.

ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ What AI should NOT Do (The "Foundations")

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Defining your Positioning
AI only knows what already exists. It cannot create your "Unique PoV" or a category-defining narrative. That requires human judgment and market understanding.
Make sure you define your positioning angle.
Use AI to debate with you on it (if needed).

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Final Messaging Sign-off
AI tends to default to "corporate fluff."
I am certain you don't want to sound like everyone else in your category. You know the WHO (it is for), WHAT (do they get) and HOW (does it happen) of your product.
Make sure you answer these in your messaging minus all the "fluff"

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Sales Pitch Strategy
Closing a $100k deal requires navigating complex buying journey and internal objections. Don't let AI navigate this for you.
Spend time with your AEs, founder(s) and define how to narrate your unique PoV in your sales conversations.

----------

Simply put,
Use AI to handle the "execution/repeated tasks".
Keep "foundations" with you.

Product Marketing needs to ensure the mindshare.
And you can't own a mind with a bot-generated soul.

Post Title: I have been working 100% remote for almost 1.5 years now
Body:
I hit the gym when most people are rushing to the office.

1ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ I hit the gym when most people are either getting ready for or commuting to the office.

2ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ I brew my own coffee 2 times a day. I absolutely love that daily ritual, especially experimenting with new varieties and brewing methods. ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ

3ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ I switch my workstations as I wish - from a chair in my side-yard to my dining table, or sometimes the sofa. Though I mostly use my WFH setup, but it's fun switching.

4ÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ£ I am overall more productive & efficient (occasional social media scrolling aside ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ). My work requires detailed research and thinking, quite environment helps me a lot.

At times, I miss interacting with people in person (I compensate by working from cafÃÂÃÂ©s sometimes ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ¬).

Post Title: Like all good things in life, Marketing ALSO takes time.
Body:
Like all good things in life, Marketing ALSO takes time.
Here's Why -

1. Your ICP doesn't wake up one day and impulsively buy a $50K platform.

2. Your buyer doesn't convert on first touch point, they need multiple interactions to start even noticing you.

3. Category creation doesn't happen overnight. It takes years of education and relentless consistency.

4. Publishing 10 blogs won't rank you #1. Months of high-value content will build authority.

5. Blasting 1000s of emails doesn't get you a conversation. Months of thoughtful nurture does.

6. That one positive conversation at the event? It turns into a deal only after multiple follow-ups.

7. You can build a target account list today. But navigating their buyer journey? That's months of work.

8. Your brand doesn't become memorable after one viral campaign. It takes repeated delivery of the same message, over-and-over, again.

If you're a B2B SaaS founder or marketer, 3 months into your marketing strategy and wondering why the needle isn't moving?

Cut yourself some slack.

Believe in your strategy, provided it's built on strong foundations.

And remember,

Like all good things in life, Marketing ALSO takes time.

Share ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂ it with your marketing folks!

--------

Talking about strong foundations, it all starts with right Positioning.

I am Arpit Purohit and I help Seed to Series A B2B SaaS startups fix their positioning, messaging and rewrite Website Homepage that actually convert + Sales Pitch Deck that close deals faster.

Post Title: If you think B2B Sales Funnel works, look at this.
Body:
If you think B2B Sales Funnel works, look at this. ÃÂ°ÃÂÃÂÃÂ
92% of B2B buyers start their journey with at least one vendor in mind.

And, 41% have ALREADY selected their preferred vendor before they even start the formal evaluation process.

And before you ask, this is an official data from Forrester's B2B Buyers' Journey Survey.

So technically,

By the time a buyer googles "Best CRM" or "Best HRMS Software"
They aren't looking for the best option.
They are looking to validate the option they already have in mind.

The "Funnel" is NOT important anymore or the nature of it has changed.

The "Day 1 List" of your buyers is the ONLY thing that matters.

So, what does this mean?

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Creating Demand > Capturing Demand

How?

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂ Educate
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂ Build trust
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂ Don't Sell, offer help
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂ Talk about their problems (not your solution)
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂ¯ÃÂ¸ÃÂ Create content that help them on their today's problems

If you do this,
When they enter the market, you are either their obvious choice,
or at least in their top consideration.

Marketing isn't just about "Capturing Demand" when people are ready to buy.
Marketing is about owning their mindshare when they are not.

If you wait for them to enter the market to say "Hello"

You are MOST LIKELY too late.

Post Title: I've deconstructed GTM from a product marketer's lens.
Body:
I've deconstructed GTM from a product marketer's lens.

Here it is in the form of The GTM GAME Canvas.

G - Game Plan (Foundations)
A - Approach (Motion)
M - Machine (Execution)
E - Evaluation (Analytics)

ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ It starts with WHO (ICP) before WHAT (channels)
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ It obsess over Positioning before Execution
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ It builds the Story before Building the machine

----

G - GAME PLAN (Foundations)

Product marketing plays a crucial role here. If this section is weak, your execution will be unfocused.

1. ICP Anchor: Who are you for?
2. Category Anchor: What market are you in?
3. Problem Narrative: What painful problem do you solve?
4. Differentiation Summary: Why are you uniquely better?

A - APPROACH (Motion)

Your high-level strategic choices about how to GTM.

1. Primary GTM Motion: Your main engine - Inbound, Outbound, PLG, Community-led, etc.
2. Secondary GTM Motion: What supports the primary GTM Motion?
3. Demand Philosophy: How do you balance Demand Creation vs Capture (95% vs. 5%)?

M - MACHINE (Execution)

Translate high-level motions into specific, measurable actions.
Fill in 3-5 of your most important plays.

For each play, connect:
- GTM Motion
- Key Channel
- Core Play (the specific tactic)
- Key Metric

Example:
Motion: Inbound-led
Channel: SEO
Core Play: Create pillar page + content cluster on "Customer Renewal Process"
Key Metric: #1-3 ranking for target keywords; # of organic MQLs

E - EVALUATION (Analytics)

How you measure success.

1. Primary Business Goal: What is your one GTM goal for the next 12 months?
2. Top 3-5 KPIs: How will you measure success?
3. GTM Tech Stack: What are the essential tools? (CRM, Automation, Outreach, etc.)

----

The reason most GTM strategies fail is because they lack clarity and connection.

This canvas forces you to:
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Connect every tactic back to your strategy
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Make explicit trade-offs (you can't do everything)
ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ Align your entire org on one page

IMO, spend 80% of our time on Section 1 "Game Plan" (Strategy Foundation)

It will guide Section 2 to 4.

Get positioning and messaging right, and everything else will become easier.

Link to the GTM GAME Canvas - https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1PcPz26KrGmCea8EhYDJTMqG2pQneW2PxqK41TwolHLw/edit?usp=sharing
